records.name_note: All admissible sources use the binomial Ilex crenata with no synonym or accepted-name conflict (NC State Extension lists only the infraspecific synonyms Ilex crenata f. genuina and Ilex crenata var. typica; RHS records Name Status: Correct). NC State describes the fruit as small black drupes, which distinguishes it from red-berried hollies such as American Holly (Ilex opaca), whose NC State page gives its fruit color as orange/red.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox lists Ilex crenata under a Poisonous to Humans heading with Poison Severity: Low, Poison Symptoms 'Minor toxicity. Ingestion may cause vomiting, diarrhea, or other illness in humans.', and Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; its Edibility line says 'Use caution. Human ingestion of berries can cause minor toxic reaction.' RHS's Potentially harmful field warns 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.', and its inline 'Pets:' label repeats the fruit warning without naming any animal. No admissible source scopes toxicity to cats or dogs specifically.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets: left null rather than inheriting Ilex opaca's (American Holly) clean cat/dog evidence — no genus-level bleed. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox page for Ilex crenata carries only a 'Poisonous to Humans' tag in its structured Problems list, with no 'Problem for Cats' or 'Problem for Dogs' tags (unlike its Ilex opaca page, which does carry both). RHS's only pet-facing caution for Ilex crenata is a generic, unscoped 'Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten' line that names no specific animal, which per the scoping rule does not support toxic_to_pets=true on its own.

soil_drainage: left null due to a genuine cross-source conflict. NC State Extension's structured tags for Ilex crenata read 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage Moist Occasionally Wet' (which would map to moderate), but Clemson HGIC's holly diseases factsheet states plainly that 'Japanese hollies (Ilex crenata) are very intolerant of poorly drained soils and are especially prone to root rot' and lists Japanese holly as 'Highly susceptible' to black root rot — a direct warning against a wet-tolerant reading. The two admissible sources disagree, so left null.

water_regime: left null due to conflicting signals. NC State Extension tags Ilex crenata '#drought tolerant' and lists it under a 'Drought Tolerant Garden' landscape theme, while Missouri Botanical Garden's structured field reads 'Water: Medium' and Clemson HGIC states that Japanese hollies (citing the 'Helleri' cultivar) 'are less tolerant of low soil moisture and benefit from consistent irrigation during drought.' These do not converge on one watering-regime enum value without guessing.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: no admissible source states an explicit numeric pH bound for Ilex crenata. NC State Extension gives only categorical buckets ('Acid (<6.0)', 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)') and RHS gives only a categorical 'Acid or Neutral' tag, neither of which is a stated numeric floor/ceiling.

chill_damage_f/day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives a temperature-based damage-onset figure or a day/night temperature range; only cold-hardiness zone/rating data exists (NC State USDA Zones 5a-8b; RHS Hardiness H6, -20 to -15°C), which per field guidance is not an actionable damage-onset temperature.

humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: NC State Extension tags Ilex crenata '#heat intolerant' and '#humidity intolerant', but these are climate-suitability warning tags (the plant struggles in regions with hot, humid summers, per MOBOT's culture note 'Plants may struggle in climates with hot, humid summers') rather than a stated ambient-humidity care requirement, so left null rather than inferring a humidity_need value from an ambiguous tag.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source gives foot-candle figures or species-specific prose stating a maximum direct-sun-hours figure for Ilex crenata; NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours...)' is the site-wide light-category legend defining the tag threshold, not a species-specific maximum, so it was not used for direct_sun_hours_max per field guidance.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule, timing, or dilution strength for Ilex crenata. Clemson HGIC's holly factsheet only cautions generally that high soil nitrogen can cause poor fruiting in hollies, with no numeric interval or month data.

soil_base: set to garden_bed based on every admissible source describing Ilex crenata solely as an in-ground landscape/hedge/foundation shrub (3-10 feet, sold and grown outdoors); no source uses container or potting-mix terminology for this species.

name_note — removed on audit: Two sub-claims are bundled; one is clean, one is uncited. (A) COVERED AND ACCURATE — "All admissible sources use the binomial Ilex crenata with no synonym or accepted-name conflict (NC State Extension lists only infraspecific synonyms)". The quote "Previously known as: Ilex crenata f. genuina Ilex crenata var. typica" is verbatim from the live NC State page, and both entries are indeed infraspecific (forma and varietas of the same binomial), not competing binomials. Independently corroborated: RHS gives "Name Status" / "Correct" and MOBOT's page is headed "Ilex crenata". (B) UNCITED-BUT-TRUE — the clause "distinguishing it from red-berried hollies such as American Holly (Ilex opaca)". The supporting quote, "Fruits are small, black, round drupes that ripen in the fall.", is verbatim from NC State's Description and supports ONLY the black-fruit half; it says nothing about Ilex opaca or red berries, and the record contains no citation to any Ilex opaca source. The comparison is factually true — NC State's Ilex opaca page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/ilex-opaca/) carries the structured field "Fruit Color: Orange Red/Burgundy" — but as written the claim label asserts a cross-species contrast its own quote does not make. Nothing here is WRONG and nothing needs dropping for falsity; the fix is either to cite the Ilex opaca page for the contrast or to trim the label. Corrected citation label: "name_note: NC State Extension describes Ilex crenata's fruit as small black drupes". Corrected field prose: "All admissible sources use the binomial Ilex crenata with no synonym or accepted-name conflict (NC State Extension lists only the infraspecific synonyms Ilex crenata f. genuina and Ilex crenata var. typica; RHS records Name Status: Correct), and the species bears black fruit — 'Fruits are small, black, round drupes that ripen in the fall.'" — appending the Ilex opaca contrast only if a citation to that page is added alongside.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: STRUCTURAL FAILURE ONLY — the value is correct, the citation coverage is not. No citation's "claim" label contains the string "scientific_name_accepted". The twelve labels cover common_name (x2), name_note (x2), is_houseplant, toxicity_detail (x2), outdoor_sun_exposure (x3) and soil_base (x2); nothing names this field, so the accepted binomial is landing uncited by the record's own labelling convention. The VALUE "Ilex crenata" is verified correct on all three live pages: NC State's H1 is "Ilex crenata" with only infraspecific entries under "Previously known as:"; MOBOT's page is headed "Ilex crenata"; and RHS's Botanical Details block ends with "Name Status" / "Correct". Repair without changing the value: extend the existing NC State naming citation's label to read "scientific_name_accepted / name_note: ...", or add an RHS citation with claim "scientific_name_accepted: RHS records Ilex crenata as the correct name" and quote "Name Status Correct" from https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/9122/ilex-crenata/details.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The substance is accurate and every quoted string is verbatim — but the field misdescribes one source's structure and trims two co-listed safety items from the other. (1) STRUCTURE SYNTHESIS: the field says RHS "under a Pets heading states 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten'". RHS has no Pets heading. The section heading on the live page is "Potentially harmful", and its single paragraph reads "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.  Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers" — "Pets:" is an inline label inside that one paragraph, not a heading. The quoted words are real; the container invented around them is not. (2) TRIMMED CO-LISTED ITEMS from the same NC State page: the record reproduces Poison Severity, Poison Symptoms, Poison Toxic Principle and Poison Part but silently drops the fourth member of that same structured block, "Causes Contact Dermatitis: No", and drops the page's separate Edibility line, "Use caution. Human ingestion of berries can cause minor toxic reaction." Both are verified live. Neither omission reverses the safety picture (the page's co-listed tags #poisonous fruits and #poisonous if ingested also point the same way, with no counter-signal tag such as a non-toxic-for-cats tag to drop), and the human-vs-pet scoping analysis is correct — but a safety field must carry the source's full list. Corrected prose: "NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox lists Ilex crenata under a Poisonous to Humans heading with Poison Severity: Low, Poison Symptoms: 'Minor toxicity. Ingestion may cause vomiting, diarrhea, or other illness in humans.', Poison Toxic Principle: Saponins, Poison Part: Fruits, and Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; the same page's Edibility field reads 'Use caution. Human ingestion of berries can cause minor toxic reaction.' — all scoped to humans, not cats or dogs. RHS, under its 'Potentially harmful' section, warns 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.' and continues, with an inline Pets label, 'Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants...'; that pets caution names no specific animal, so per the cat/dog scoping rule it does not establish toxic_to_pets=true and the field is left null rather than inferred." No source disagreement on edibility exists to disclose — NC State, RHS and MOBOT are consistent.

The species epithet 'vomitoria': NC State states Native Americans used the leaves to make 'a ceremonial emetic drink which, when consumed in large quantities, caused the purging indicated by the specific epithet.' Clemson corroborates the leaves' historical ceremonial/trade use and caffeine content but does not repeat the purgative-epithet explanation directly. NC State also notes the common name 'yaupon' derives from Catawban, and that modern-day young leaves can be browned, dried, and steeped to make caffeinated Yaupon tea.

Reported mature height varies by source: NC State gives 10-20.5 ft, Clemson gives 3-15 ft for South Carolina, and UF/IFAS ask.ifas.ufl.edu gives 15-25 ft - left out of the schema since no numeric height field exists to record it, but noted here as a real cross-source spread rather than a single settled figure.

No admissible source gave an explicit watering-cadence statement, a numeric soil pH range, fertilizer guidance, chill-damage onset temperature, humidity target, or light level in foot-candles for this species, so those fields are left null rather than inferred from genus-level or general holly knowledge.

No bleed confirmed from the American Holly (Ilex opaca) or other Ilex records: all citations here are drawn only from pages specifically about Ilex vomitoria (or its cultivars), not from Ilex opaca or genus-level 'Holly' pages, except Clemson's general 'Holly' factsheet, which was read narrowly for its Ilex-vomitoria-specific passages only.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: REFUTED on three counts, one of them a source misattribution. (1) MISATTRIBUTED SCOPE. The field states that RHS's "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." appears "under a 'Pets' heading that names no specific animal," and the matching citation label says the same. That is wrong. On the live RHS page the field label is "Potentially harmful", and its value runs: "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.  Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". The quoted sentence pair is verbatim, but it is the GENERAL potentially-harmful text; the "Pets:" sub-entry is a different, separate string that does NOT contain the gloves sentence. Corrected wording: 'RHS's "Potentially harmful" field warns "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling."; a separate "Pets:" sub-entry repeats only the fruit warning — "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers" — and names no animal.' (2) DROPPED CO-LISTED TAG. NC State's poison block co-lists "Causes Contact Dermatitis: No" immediately beside the severity, symptoms and toxic principle the record does reproduce. The record carries RHS's protective-equipment warning but silently drops NC State's explicit no-dermatitis tag, which is exactly the one-sided trim the co-listed-tag rule forbids, and it hides a genuine source disagreement on handling risk (RHS says wear gloves; NC State says the plant does not cause contact dermatitis). Both must appear. (3) UNDISCLOSED EDIBILITY SPLIT. NC State's own "Edibility:" field reads "The young leaves may be picked, browned and dried in an oven, steeped in hot water and used to make Yaupon tea. It contains caffeine." while its Poison Part is "Fruits". A safety field should state that split explicitly — leaves used for tea, fruit the poisonous part — rather than leaving the tea fact stranded in unknowns. Separately, a structural gap for repair: the field asserts severity "low" and scope "fruit", but no citation quote carries either; the page prints "Poison Severity:" / "Low" and "Poison Part:" / "Fruits", which should be quoted. (a) Undisclosed contradicting tag: the MOBOT species page (taxonid=287336, cited twice in this record) carries the structured line "Water: Medium" in its tag block, directly above the Culture paragraph the record quotes from. That rating appears nowhere in the citations or the unknowns. (b) Cadence read off a trait, not a prescription: citation 12's label asserts "water_regime is dry_thoroughly_between" on the strength of "once established-will tolerate drought." That quote is verbatim (NC State: "and-once established-will tolerate drought"), but drought SURVIVAL once established is not a watering PRESCRIPTION to let the root zone dry out fully between waterings — the same category error as reading a hardiness zone as a damage-onset temperature. (c) The sources actually prescribe against drying out: MOBOT says "Plants are tolerant of full sun as long as soils are not allowed to dry out, but generally appreciate protection from hot sun and drying winds" and prescribes "moderately but evenly moist" soils; UF/IFAS hedges its drought claim ("Camellias are FAIRLY drought tolerant but need irrigation during extended dry periods" — the record's own prose drops that "fairly" and quotes NC State's unhedged "tolerate drought") and prescribes "1 inch of water per week during flowering," which for sasanqua is a 4-6 week October-December bloom; NC State's drainage tags pair "Moist" with "Good Drainage"; UF/IFAS's planting guidance is to mulch 2-3 inches to "conserve moisture in the root zone." (d) Correct token: the middle-of-scale token — the water_regime analogue of the moderate landing this same record correctly chose for soil_drainage — i.e. water when the top of the root zone has dried but never let the root zone dry through. NOT dry_thoroughly_between, and equally not a wet/constantly-moist token (UF/IFAS's "sensitive to overwatering and succumb to root rot when kept too wet" rules that out). At repair time the MOBOT "Water: Medium" tag must be cited or disclosed, not left out.

water_regime left null: NC State's 'once established will tolerate drought' is a survival trait, not a cadence; MOBOT rates the species 'Water: Medium' and says soils should not be allowed to dry out; UF/IFAS calls camellias only 'fairly' drought tolerant and prescribes 1 inch of water weekly during flowering -- no single token fits without picking a side.

soil_ph_max — removed on audit: REFUTED — the value contradicts its own citation, and it repeats an error this catalog has already reversed twice on audit. The live page's Soil pH block is exactly "Alkaline (>8.0)" and "Neutral (6.0-8.0)". Citation[10]'s quote is verbatim, but its claim literally reads "structured Soil pH tag lists Alkaline as greater than 8.0" — a citation for an OPEN-ENDED band above 8.0 being used to justify a ceiling of exactly 8.0. 8.0 is the FLOOR of the alkaline band, not its top; recording max=8 silently discards the alkaline tolerance the citation was added to establish. This is the identical defect the catalog already caught and fixed elsewhere on the same tag pair: b4 Lavender's unknowns records "soil_ph_max: removed by audit. The stored 8.0 was wrong in the harmful direction - both cited sources describe alkaline soil above 8.0 as tolerated or preferred, and an open-ended top band yields no defensible ceiling," and b7 Thyme's records "soil_ph_max — removed on audit: … The '>8.0' tag means the source considers pH above 8.0 ALSO tolerated (an open-ended band)." Five other records on this exact tag pair (b1 Snake Plant, b13 Baby's Breath, b13 Cosmos, b16 Candytuft, b16 Bee delphinium) all carry soil_ph_max null. The one nearby record that legitimately holds 8 is b39 Tatarian Dogwood — and its own unknowns explain why it is different: "NC State's own Soil pH field lists only 'Acid (<6.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' (not 'Alkaline'), giving an upper bound (8.0…)." Cornus sericea DOES carry the Alkaline tag, so that exemption does not apply. CORRECTED VALUE: soil_ph_max = null. Drop citation[10] as a soil_ph_max citation (or re-label it as evidence of open-ended alkaline tolerance) and add an unknowns entry along the lines of: "soil_ph_max: NC State tags both Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0) for this species; the alkaline band is open-ended with no stated ceiling, so no maximum could be sourced without inventing one."

water_dry_down_target — removed on audit: REFUTED — the second clause adds a scope no source carries and contradicts a quote elsewhere in this same record. Citation[12]'s quote is verified verbatim in MOBOT's Culture section: "Best grown in organically rich, fertile, consistently moist soils in full sun to part shade." That sentence supports "keep soil consistently moist." It says nothing about waterings, intervals, or dry-down. The field's added clause — "avoid letting it dry out between waterings" — is an inference, and it is in direct tension with the record's own citation[7] quote from NC State: "Although it tolerates a range of soil conditions, including wet and dry sites and heavy clay soil…" plus the page's "Occasionally Dry" drainage tag and "#dry soils tolerant" tag. It also imports container-culture framing ("between waterings") onto a plant this record correctly classifies as an in-ground garden_bed shrub; landscape shrubs are not watered on a between-waterings cycle. The catalog has already ruled on this exact pattern for the sibling species: b39 Tatarian Dogwood left water_dry_down_target null with the reason "No admissible source frames watering in terms of a container-style soil check depth, dry-down interval, or days-between-watering estimate; guidance is limited to soil-moisture-preference language … which was used for water_regime and soil_drainage but does not map onto these container-culture fields." CORRECTED VALUE: preferred fix is null, matching b39, with that reasoning moved into unknowns. If the field is kept, trim to the sourced clause only: "Prefers organically rich, consistently moist soil." — and drop "avoid letting it dry out between waterings."

outdoor_sun_exposure — FLAGGED on audit (left as-is, needs manual review before landing): REFUTE the 'full_shade' entry only. 'full_sun' and 'part_shade' should STAY; 'full_shade' should GO, leaving ["full_sun","part_shade"]. Quote verification first, so this is not mistaken for a fabrication finding: Penn State's "Light Requirements: sun, part shade, shade" is a REAL, literal, species-specific structured field — I found it verbatim twice inside the Nymphaea odorata blocks (alongside "Water Body Type: bog, pond bottom, shallow water, water garden", "Water Quality Needs: somewhat acidic", "Hardiness Zones: 4 to 8"). Nothing here is synthesized. The defect is value-level over-reach on one token plus undisclosed source conflict. Two other admissible sources contradict a shade reading, and the record cites one of them while hiding the disagreement: RHS's species page gives "Position Full sun" with no shade option and its species-specific cultivation prose says "Grow in undisturbed water in full sun."; NC State Extension's Nymphaea page carries the structured pair "Light: Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day) / Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)" — no deep/full-shade token — with prose "Most prefer full sun, but some will tolerate some shade." Missouri Botanical Garden's hardy water lily guidance likewise floors it around three hours of sun, which is part shade, not full shade. Landing full_shade in a care app tells a user a water lily will grow in full shade, which the only species-specific cultivation prose in the citation set flatly denies. Second, separate defect in the same field: the citation label "RHS's Aspect/Light field" misnames the source field. RHS has no 'Light' field, and its actual "Aspect" field reads "South–facing or West–facing" — a different value entirely. "Full sun" comes from RHS's "Position" field. Corrected citation wording: claim "outdoor_sun_exposure full_sun is supported by RHS's structured Position field for this species", quote "Full sun" — or better, use the cultivation sentence "Grow in undisturbed water in full sun." Third, the record must disclose the disagreement (the way name_note discloses the naming split): Penn State's tag list admits 'shade' while RHS and NC State cap this species at full sun / partial shade, and the catalog is following the latter.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Two defects, one of them a safety trim and one a scope problem. (1) TRIMMED HANDLING WARNING. The page's Poison Symptoms value ends with a sentence the record drops in both the quote and the field prose. Actual full page text: "Salivation and nasal discharge, sweating, tingling sensation, headache, depression, weakness, abdominal pain, nausea vomiting, coma, low blood pressure, death. Ingestion of a few leaves can cause serious problems." The record stops at "death." — the dropped clause is the single most actionable line in the block for a pet owner (it quantifies the dose). (2) UNDISCLOSED SCOPE. In the page HTML the Poison Severity / Poison Symptoms / Poison Toxic Principle / Causes Contact Dermatitis / Poison Part fields all sit inside one block under the group heading "Poisonous to Humans:", entirely separate from the "Problems:" block that carries "Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs / Problem for Horses". The record presents that human-poisoning severity and symptom list ('headache', 'tingling sensation', 'low blood pressure') as if it were the pet profile, and states "NC State rates poison severity as High for this species" without saying the rating is human-scoped. NC State publishes no severity or symptom list scoped to cats or dogs. (3) Minor: the co-listed field "Causes Contact Dermatitis: No" from the same block is dropped. Everything else checks out verbatim — "Poison Severity: High", "Poison Toxic Principle: Andromedotoxin", "Poison Part: Flowers, Leaves", and the three Problem-for tags all match the live page. No source disagreement on edibility exists to disclose. Suggested repair wording: "NC State lists this species under a 'Poisonous to Humans' block: Poison Severity High, toxic principle Andromedotoxin, poisonous parts Flowers and Leaves, Causes Contact Dermatitis No. The full symptom text is: 'Salivation and nasal discharge, sweating, tingling sensation, headache, depression, weakness, abdominal pain, nausea vomiting, coma, low blood pressure, death. Ingestion of a few leaves can cause serious problems.' Separately, under 'Problems', the same page tags the plant as a Problem for Cats, a Problem for Dogs, and a Problem for Horses; NC State gives no separate severity or symptom list scoped to cats or dogs."
